planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Monstera Albo needs strong, consistent light on its white variegated sections, which cannot photosynthesize and rely on the green portions of each leaf.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Monstera Albo needs strong, consistent light on its white variegated sections, which cannot photosynthesize and rely on the green portions of each leaf. Large, deeply fenestrated leaves are boldly marked with irregular patches, streaks, or entirely half-white sectors of pure white variegation against the classic glossy green Swiss cheese plant leaf, a chimeric, genetically unstable pattern that varies unpredictably from leaf to leaf and has made well-variegated specimens among the most sought-after and expensive houseplants in the world. Because the white tissue contains no chlorophyll, plants with heavy variegation grow more slowly and are more prone to stress than solid-green monstera, and stems can revert to solid green or, less often, produce leaves with too little chlorophyll to sustain themselves. Provide bright indirect light to support the reduced photosynthetic area, prune out any fully white, unsustainable growth, and propagate stem cuttings that include at least some variegated leaf tissue to preserve the pattern.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Monstera Aurea needs strong, consistent light on its yellow variegated sections, which contribute less to photosynthesis than the green portions.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Monstera Aurea needs strong, consistent light on its yellow variegated sections, which contribute less to photosynthesis than the green portions. Large, deeply fenestrated leaves are marked with bold, irregular patches of bright golden-yellow variegation against deep green, a warmer-toned counterpart to the more famous white-variegated Monstera Albo, similarly prized by collectors for its rarity and unpredictable, genetically unstable variegation pattern. Like other variegated monstera, plants with heavy yellow sectoring grow more slowly than solid-green plants and are more vulnerable to stress, and stems can revert to solid green over time if not selectively propagated from variegated growth. Provide bright indirect light, prune out any reverted all-green growth if maintaining variegation is the goal, and propagate from stem cuttings that retain variegated leaf tissue.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; hot dog cactus stores water in its jointed segments and rots quickly in wet or dense soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; hot dog cactus stores water in its jointed segments and rots quickly in wet or dense soil. Thick, gray-green, jointed stem segments stack end to end like a string of plump sausages or candles, an unmistakably quirky, sculptural form that gives this South African succulent both of its playful common names, with small clusters of leaves appearing briefly at the growing tips before dropping in the plant's natural dry-season dormancy. It cycles through periods of active growth and leaf drop tied to seasonal moisture availability in its native habitat, so leafless, dormant-looking segments in a home setting are often normal rather than a sign of poor health, especially when watering is reduced in winter. Water sparingly, more so during active growth and much less when the plant appears to be resting, and provide bright light to keep the segmented stems from stretching.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Krimson Queen hoya colors most vividly in bright light and blooms most reliably when slightly pot-bound.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Krimson Queen hoya colors most vividly in bright light and blooms most reliably when slightly pot-bound. Thick, waxy, oval leaves are edged in broad creamy-white margins that blush distinctly pink in bright light, especially on new growth, growing on vigorous, twining vines that eventually produce rounded clusters of small, star-shaped, fragrant pink flowers with a deep red center from the same reusable flowering spurs year after year. One of the most popular variegated hoya cultivars for its reliable, colorful foliage even when not in bloom, it climbs or trails readily and rewards a bright window with steady growth and repeat flowering. Provide a trellis or hanging basket for the twining stems, let the potting mix dry between waterings, and never remove the woody flowering spurs, which continue to rebloom for years.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Hindu Rope hoya is slow-growing and blooms most reliably when left undisturbed and slightly pot-bound for years.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Hindu Rope hoya is slow-growing and blooms most reliably when left undisturbed and slightly pot-bound for years. Thick, waxy leaves curl and twist tightly along densely contorted stems that coil like braided rope, an unusual crinkled mutation of the common wax plant that gives this cultivar a sculptural, almost knotted texture unlike any other hoya, eventually producing the same fragrant, star-shaped pink flower clusters as the straight species once mature. Slow-growing and long-lived, it is a classic heirloom houseplant often passed down through generations, thriving for decades in the same pot with minimal repotting, since disturbing an established, pot-bound plant can set back or delay flowering for years. Let the potting mix dry between waterings, provide bright indirect light, and resist the urge to repot frequently, since this cultivar flowers best when left undisturbed.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference
